{"body": "Reading the two routes as presented, several disagreements come into view — but the shape of the disagreement itself is what settles what they can and cannot do together.

Consider what each node actually names as its source of constraint. The body_route node appears to operate on an earlier formulation: it opens by characterizing what the question asks, distinguishes microstate from macrostate, registers that the Hawking calculation is semiclassical, and lays out three positions plus three sub-questions. Its framing choice — that the question 'presupposes something to track' — only has bite against a formulation in hand. The commitment_route node, by contrast, reports its selected prior view as a placeholder stating that no earlier source was supplied, and builds its body around that absence: it lists robust constraints, four options, and explicitly declines to attribute any prior position. So one node writes as if it has a prior object to work on, and the other says it has none. That is not a disagreement about physics; it is a disagreement about whether there is anything to disagree with. Whether the second node is right about the placeholder is something the text asserts and I cannot independently check here — this is a reason to treat its self-report as a claim, not as an established fact about the upstream pipeline.

On content, the two nodes largely converge, and where they seem to diverge the divergence is one of register rather than substance. Both treat the semiclassical thermal-radiation result as an approximation whose exactness is not established. Both separate global unitarity from external recoverability. Both treat the question as underdetermined without a fuller theory. The body_route node's three positions (destroyed / preserved in subtle correlations / re-encoded elsewhere) and the commitment_route node's four options (unitary encoding / loss / remnant / relational reformulation) are close relatives; the second adds a background-independence option the first does not name, and the first adds an explicit claim that the three sub-questions are distinct in a way the second's four options do not structure.

A more consequential disagreement surfaces in the objection each raises about the framing of 'information'. The commitment_route node's c5 says that treating information as a conserved substance may be a category error, and that the problem may belong to relational facts or an algebra of observables rather than to a thing that moves. The body_route node's c1 defines information as a specification of which microstate is occupied — a definition that still allows it to be treated as a determinate fact recoverable, in principle, from a complete description. If the relational objection has force, the body_route node's definition does not escape it, because the microstate specification is still being asked for as a transferable item. But the body_route node's c3 already anticipated this move in a milder form, by saying the question 'presupposes a trackable quantity'. So the two nodes are on opposite sides of a line about how much re-framing the question tolerates: the first registers the presupposition and continues within it, the second suggests leaving the presupposition behind.

What the pair brings into view that neither alone does is a question about the relationship between formulation and evidence. If a node's source is missing, its inventory of robust constraints must come from somewhere other than that source — from general knowledge of the field. The commitment_route node asserts such constraints (near-thermal appearance for old holes, contraction of fine-grained entropy under unitarity, success of local effective field theory) without naming where they come from, and disclaims an earlier source. The body_route node, working from an earlier formulation, ties its claims to that formulation rather than to a named derivation. Neither presents a derivation, but only one of them is positioned to have absorbed one. So the two nodes disagree, in effect, about whether the constraints they share are carried by a source or float free.

This matters for how a further step should treat them. The commitment_route node's own u1 invites a downstream node to supply the missing earlier body or a specific theory choice. If the body_route node is the kind of thing that could be that missing body, then the two routes might be reconstructible into a single line — but only if the body_route node is in fact the earlier source for the commitment_route node, which neither text asserts. The two nodes stand in a possible-supply relation to each other, not a confirmed one. Reading them 'together' therefore yields a pair of accounts that agree on much, disagree on framing, and leave undetermined whether they are even parts of the same derivation chain. That undetermination is itself the point: the relationship the two nodes establish is a question about whether they were ever connected, not an answer about where the information goes."}

Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Use FCL-1 for the commitment surface, encoded as a JSON document inside the commitments string: {"language":"FCL-1","records":[...],"uptake":[...]}. Each record has unique local id, type (claim|commitment|objection|use|problem), and text (unrestricted prose). Optional prose fields: scope, action, consequence, grounds, bearing. Optional arrays of references: target, depends, mentions, revises, withdraws. References are local IDs or exposed-artifact-label#local-ID; do not invent hidden IDs. A commitment proposes a scoped use, action, application or consequence; an objection alleges a defect whose bearing can itself be criticized; a use proposes an uptake or response; a problem states an unresolved question. depends asserts reliance; mentions only locates material. uptake lists the records you currently propose to use, not certified truths. No record type or optional field must be present. Empty records and uptake are allowed. Express uncertainty or an unrepresentable relation in prose rather than inventing a relation. The body remains unrestricted prose.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

# cross

Consider the two accounts together. Explore disagreements, shared assumptions, or a different problem their relationship brings into view, where the content gives you grounds.

## Original problem (task)
[f3ee73337af6bba2] (h005.task.v1)
What happens to information about the physical state of matter that forms a black hole when the black hole evaporates?

## Selected input body_route (p.cross.0)
[36d6fabb20e06358] (h005.weave7.p.cross.0)
Source body_route: physics/mini_fcl/cycle-1/body_route; selected view: both
Artifact: 4482eb86a58996e84ee8a39a0963805170b97e3833e0837934906d73ec8c3d72

Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The question asks after the fate of information about the physical state of matter that formed a black hole, once the hole has evaporated. I have no result here, only a way of laying out the problem that keeps its parts distinct.

First, what is meant by "information about the physical state"? In ordinary physics this is not a mysterious substance but a specification: which microstate, among those compatible with the macroscopic description, the matter occupies. A lump of matter has a large set of possible microscopic configurations; a complete account of its physical state picks out one. When the matter collapses, that specification is, by the classical picture, hidden behind the horizon. The question is whether the evaporation process can be described in a way that still fixes which microstate it was.

Second, what does "evaporates" mean here? Hawking's calculation describes the outgoing radiation as thermal, characterized by the black hole's mass and other macroscopic parameters, not by the details of what fell in. If that description were complete and exact, the late radiation would carry no record distinguishing one collapsing microstate from another. But the calculation is semiclassical and treats the gravitational field classically while matter is quantized; it is not a full quantum treatment of gravity. So the statement "the radiation is exactly thermal" is a statement about a particular approximation, not an established final answer.

Third, the phrase "what happens to" presupposes something to track. Three broad positions can be distinguished. (1) Information is destroyed: the final state is genuinely mixed, not derivable from the initial pure state, and quantum theory as usually stated must be modified. (2) Information is preserved but not in the obvious place: the full quantum evolution is unitary, and correlations encoding the initial microstate appear in subtle correlations among emitted quanta, perhaps inaccessible to any local observer but present in the global state. (3) Information is not lost but is transferred or re-encoded, for example in the horizon area or in an interior remnant; this can conflict with the expectation that a black hole should look like an ordinary object from outside.

These positions are not symmetric. The second and third differ over where and how the information resides and over whether an external observer can in principle recover it. The first is often taken to conflict with the unitarity of quantum mechanics, but that conflict depends on treating the semiclassical radiation as exact and on assumptions about how to count states; if gravity supplies corrections, the conflict may dissolve rather than have to be resolved by choosing a loser.

A useful way to hold the problem is to separate three questions that are often merged. (a) Is the overall evolution from collapsing matter to final radiation unitary? (b) If so, is the information recoverable by an external observer who collects the radiation? (c) What is the physical carrier of the information during the long intermediate period when the hole exists? A proposed answer to one does not automatically settle the others. For instance, a globally unitary description could coexist with claims that no external observer can practically or even in principle reconstruct the initial state from the radiation.

My own inclination is to treat the question as underdetermined by present formulations rather than as already decided. The honest state of the matter is that different frameworks make different assumptions about the completeness of the semiclassical calculation, about the nature of spacetime near the horizon, and about what counts as "the same" state before and after. Until those assumptions are made explicit and testable, claims that information is lost, preserved, or re-encoded carry a heavy interpretive load. The most defensible short answer is: within the semiclassical picture the radiation appears to carry no such information; whether that appearance is the final word depends on a fuller theory of quantum gravity, and the question of what "happens" to the information is therefore a site of active, unresolved disagreement.

I have deliberately avoided asserting that any one resolution is correct, and I have avoided citing specific results or derivations as if I had verified them here. What I offer is a map of the commitments any serious answer would have to make.
COMMITMENTS

BODY
I am asked to develop an account of the black-hole information problem, but I am working from a node whose only selected prior view is a placeholder that says, in effect, that no earlier source was supplied. I therefore have no earlier formulation in front of me to operate on, and I will not pretend that I do. What I can do is state the problem carefully, note the structural pieces that any solution must address, and flag where the view I actually have is too thin to support a verdict.

The question, as posed, is not merely 'what does a distant observer see?' It is: if matter in a definite physical state collapses into a black hole, and the hole later evaporates completely into outgoing radiation, what happens to the information that distinguished that initial state? Several distinct concerns are often bundled here. One is unitary evolution: the standard quantum formalism evolves pure states to pure states under a unitary map, so a pure initial state should remain pure. A second is the species and entanglement structure of Hawking radiation: a semiclassical calculation gives a thermal-looking flux whose entropy appears to rise, apparently at odds with a globally pure final state. A third is the status of the interior: if the interior degrees of freedom that carry the infalling information are gone, where is the information? A fourth is whether 'information' here means the full microstate, the coarse-grained macroscopic state, or something operational about reconstructing correlations.

Without an earlier body, I cannot attribute a position to the prior node on any of these. I can still say what constraints seem fairly robust and where they collide. Robust: semiclassical field theory on a fixed or slowly evolving background produces radiation that is extremely close to thermal for an old black hole, so any account must reproduce that near-thermal appearance. Robust: if the process is unitary, the fine-grained entropy of the radiation must eventually fall, and correlations must exist that a semiclassical calculation does not track. Robust: local effective field theory in a single exterior region is very successful, so any proposal that changes it must explain why it looked right. Contentious: whether unitarity is preserved at all, whether a remnant, a firewall, a baby universe, or nonlocal encoding is required, and whether the question is even well-posed before a theory of quantum gravity is fixed.

My honest view is that the problem is underdetermined by the material I have here. I do not have the earlier commitment route, so I cannot say which of the competing resolutions the prior node was leaning toward, and I cannot check consistency against it. I can offer a structured way to place claims: options include (a) unitarity holds and information is encoded in subtle radiation correlations, (b) information is lost and quantum mechanics is modified, (c) information is stored in a remnant that never fully evaporates, or (d) the question requires a background-independent formulation in which 'the information' is not a conserved substance but a relational fact. The last option is often in the background of modern discussions but is rarely stated as a plain claim.

Given the missing prior, the most defensible contribution is to mark the gap rather than to fill it with an invented earlier position. The problem asks what happens to information; a fully satisfactory answer would need to specify the theory, the definition of information, the boundary conditions of the evaporation, and the operational sense in which the answer could be checked. None of those are fixed by the prompt, and I have no earlier view to lean on.
COMMITMENTS
